venues.a: Merrion Square — Upper Merrion Street, opposite Government Buildings
venues.d: Four restored Georgian townhouses facing the government buildings — Dublin's definitive grand hotel, with the country's only two-star kitchen downstairs.

venues.a: St Stephen's Green — Grafton Street quarter
venues.d: The 'Grande Dame' of Dublin, open since 1824 on St Stephen's Green — where the Irish Constitution was drafted, and still the city's most storied address.

venues.a: Grafton Street — Balfe Street, off the main shopping street
venues.d: The Doyle Collection's Dublin flagship, tucked just off Grafton Street — a polished, art-filled house at the very centre of the city's shopping and dining.
A striking checkerboard-faced design hotel on Grand Canal Square, run by Anantara — the city's best rooftop bar and a genuine spa with infinity pool.

venues.a: Ballsbridge — Eastmoreland Place, a quiet Georgian lane
venues.d: A flamboyant boutique house in a red-brick Victorian former nurses' home, on a leafy lane near the canal — the most characterful small luxury stay in the city.

venues.a: Dublin 2 — Adelaide Road, by the Iveagh Gardens
venues.d: A restored red-brick Victorian townhouse of forty-odd rooms near the Iveagh Gardens — an intimate, characterful boutique with a lovely gin-and-tea parlour.

venues.a: St Stephen's Green — Earlsfort Terrace, by the National Concert Hall
venues.d: A polished, well-run Hilton-luxury house opposite the National Concert Hall — dependable five-star comfort a moment from St Stephen's Green.

venues.a: Ballsbridge — Simmonscourt Road, in two acres of gardens
venues.d: A calm, generously scaled hotel set in two acres of private gardens in leafy Ballsbridge — the most spacious luxury stay, with a proper pool and spa.

venues.a: Merrion Square — within The Merrion, Upper Merrion Street
venues.d: Ireland's most celebrated restaurant — over forty years at the top, and the country's only two-star table for most of that time, inside The Merrion.

venues.a: Dublin 1 — Parnell Square, by the Writers Museum
venues.d: Finnish chef Mickael Viljanen's precise, luxurious cooking in a Georgian basement north of the Liffey — a benchmark two-star table.

venues.a: Blackrock — inside Blackrock Market, south county Dublin
venues.d: A tiny, surprise tasting-menu room hidden in Blackrock Market — deeply personal cooking built around the five tastes, and now two stars.
Fire-fed, fiercely seasonal sharing plates cooked over open flame in full view — a relaxed, tablecloth-free one-star that feels like a great neighbourhood room.

venues.a: Ballsbridge — Sussex Terrace, by the canal
venues.d: John and Sandy Wyer's pared-back, ingredient-led cooking near the canal — a likeable, quietly excellent room newly promoted to one star.
A stylish, understated neighbourhood one-star run with real conviction — seasonal Irish cooking that balances contrasting flavours beautifully.

venues.a: St Stephen's Green — first floor of The Fitzwilliam, over the Green
venues.d: Andy McFadden's refined French-rooted cooking on the first floor of The Fitzwilliam — a graceful one-star room overlooking St Stephen's Green.

venues.a: Dublin 2 — D'Olier Street, by Trinity College
venues.d: A stylish, buzzy one-star from a well-known Dublin kitchen partnership — considered, contemporary cooking a step from Trinity.

venues.a: Grafton Street quarter — Trinity Street, Dublin 2
venues.d: A modern brasserie blending French influences with contemporary Irish cooking — a Bib Gourmand for well over a decade running, and a reliable Dublin favourite.
A stripped-back, Mediterranean-leaning bistro from the team behind Etto — small plates, a smart wine list and a Bib Gourmand for real value.
A warm neighbourhood room built around a charcoal grill and family-style sharing plates — a long-standing Bib Gourmand in Dublin 8.
Chinese and Taiwanese sharing plates that won a Bib Gourmand in 2026 — the inspectors singled out the pulled-beef wu ya bao as 'lip-smackingly delicious'.
An osteria-style Italian built around informality and honest pricing — ingredient-led, simple pleasures, and a new Bib Gourmand for 2026.

venues.a: Ballsbridge — above M. O'Brien's pub, Sussex Terrace
venues.d: The Wyers' rustic little bistro above a Dublin pub — pâté de campagne, coq au vin and other French comforts done beautifully, with a 2026 Bib Gourmand.

venues.n: Trinity College & the Book of Kells Experience
venues.d: Ireland's oldest university, its cobbled squares reached through an arch that has stood since 1592. The 9th-century Book of Kells sits at the heart of a reimagined digital experience, after which you climb into the barrel-vaulted Old Library. A private early-access guide spares multi-generational groups the queue and the crush.

A 65-metre corridor of oak and marble busts, the most photographed library chamber in the world. Its books are being carefully removed in a conservation project running to 2027, and Luke Jerram's illuminated seven-metre Gaia globe currently floats at its centre. See it now, in this rare transitional state.

Seven centuries of power on one site, from a Viking-age fortress to the Georgian State Apartments where Irish presidents are still inaugurated. A private guided tour takes in the medieval undercroft and the ornate St Patrick's Hall, an easy, cultured morning for a family.

Ireland's museum of world cultures, and one of Europe's finest, gifted by an American mining magnate. Illuminated Qurans, the oldest known fragments of the New Testament, Chinese jade and Japanese scrolls sit side by side. Free to enter, blissfully uncrowded, with a rooftop garden and a good vegetarian-friendly café.

Dublin's oldest building, founded around 1030 by the Viking king Sitric, with a vast medieval crypt beneath the nave, the largest in Britain or Ireland. The mummified cat and rat found in an organ pipe, nicknamed Tom and Jerry, are an oddly charming detail for children.

The largest church in Ireland, built beside the well where St Patrick is said to have baptised converts. Jonathan Swift, author of Gulliver's Travels, was dean here and lies buried in the nave. Time your visit for choral evensong, sung by a choir that has performed here for over 500 years.

Seven floors rising through a glass atrium shaped like a giant pint, ending at the Gravity Bar, 46 metres up with a 360-degree sweep of the city. Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease here in 1759. A private tasting and a table at the top can be arranged away from the tour crowds.

The original 1780 distillery, now a slick whiskey experience with guided tastings and blend-your-own sessions. For serious collectors, private premium tastings pour rare and cask-strength expressions rarely seen outside Ireland.

The prison where the leaders of the 1916 Easter Rising were held and executed, a place that shaped modern Ireland. The vast Victorian East Wing, ringed by tiered iron galleries, is unforgettable. Tickets sell out weeks ahead, so a guide who secures timed entry is invaluable.

Bronze Age gold hoards, the eerily preserved Iron Age bog bodies, and the Ardagh Chalice and Tara Brooch, the finest surviving Celtic metalwork. A short, well-curated visit that gives real depth to everything else you see in Ireland.

A serene collection running from Fra Angelico and Vermeer to a whole room of Jack B. Yeats, brother of the poet. Caravaggio's The Taking of Christ, lost for centuries and rediscovered in a Dublin Jesuit house, is the quiet showstopper. Free entry, elegant galleries, unhurried.

A fully interactive museum in the vaults of a old bonded warehouse, tracing how ten million Irish emigrants shaped the world. Engaging and high-tech, it is a favourite with teenagers and works beautifully for a curious family.

A jewel-box townhouse museum of 20th-century Dublin, reopened in 2025 after a €4m restoration, including a whole room devoted to U2. Its guided storytelling tours, capped at small groups, are among the most charming hours in the city.

A perfectly kept Victorian park at the head of Grafton Street, with a lake, a bandstand and Yeats and Joyce memorials among the flowerbeds. The ideal breather between shopping and museums, and a green lung for children to run in.

The finest Georgian square in the city, ringed by red-brick townhouses with their famous rainbow of front doors and delicate fanlights. Oscar Wilde grew up here, and his reclining statue lounges in the garden opposite. A gentle, photogenic walk through Dublin's most refined quarter.

Dublin's pedestrianised shopping spine, lined with buskers and the grand Brown Thomas department store for luxury houses and Irish designers. Nearby Powerscourt Townhouse, a converted Georgian mansion, hides boutiques and cafés under its glass roof.

The cobbled cultural quarter is genuinely charming in daylight, for the Saturday food market, galleries, and independent shops, and best avoided as a boisterous, overpriced pub scene after dark. Come mid-morning for the atmosphere without the stag parties.

The cast-iron pedestrian bridge of 1816, once charged a halfpenny to cross, is the Liffey's most-loved landmark. A slow riverside walk along the quays, past the Custom House and the Famine memorial statues, threads the city's history together.

One of Europe's largest enclosed city parks, seven times the size of London's Hyde Park, with herds of wild fallow deer roaming freely. It holds the President's residence, the towering Papal Cross, and open space that feels a world away from the city.

One of the world's oldest zoos, dating to 1831, now a spacious modern conservation park with an African savanna and an Asian elephant herd. A reliable, well-run day out for younger children within the greenery of Phoenix Park.

The President of Ireland's official residence, a white Georgian mansion open for free guided tours on Saturdays by ticketed lottery. A rare glimpse inside a working head-of-state house for those who plan ahead.

The world's first cemetery museum, set in a Victorian garden cemetery where Michael Collins, Daniel O'Connell and Éamon de Valera lie. Superb guided tours bring the 1916 Rising and Civil War alive, and the restored O'Connell Tower gives a 222-step view over the city.

Ireland's leading modern-art museum, housed in the magnificent 17th-century Royal Hospital Kilmainham with formal gardens. Contemporary shows in a serene classical setting, an easy pairing with the neighbouring Kilmainham Gaol.

venues.n: National Museum of Ireland – Decorative Arts & History (Collins Barracks)
venues.d: A former army barracks now filled with Irish silver, furniture, fashion and a moving exhibition on the events of 1916. Quieter than the Kildare Street museum, and a fine complement to it.

The General Post Office was the headquarters of the 1916 Rising, its pillars still pocked with bullet marks. The immersive witness-history museum inside explains the birth of the Republic, on the city's grand central boulevard beneath the soaring Spire.
A hands-on recreation of Viking and medieval Dublin, right beside Christ Church. Light, playful and genuinely educational, it is one of the best stops in the city for families with younger children.

Beside the cathedral sits Ireland's first public library, opened in 1707 and almost unchanged since, with dark oak stacks and rare volumes in wired reading cages. A hushed, scholarly secret loved by bibliophiles.

A genuine spit-and-sawdust pub where musicians gather for informal trad sessions, fiercely protected from the tourist circuit by its owners. This is the real thing, warm, unpolished and unforgettable, best experienced with a local who knows the room.

A fishing village on a rugged headland, thirty minutes by coastal train, with a cliff walk over the Irish Sea, seals in the harbour, and some of the freshest seafood near Dublin. A superb half-day escape, with a private car easily arranged for those who prefer not to take the train.

Dublin's Beverly Hills, a genteel seaside village of a medieval castle, artisan cafés and celebrity residents, with the Vico Road viewpoint often likened to the Bay of Naples. Discreet, moneyed and lovely, exactly the sort of place a member might quietly settle.

An elegant Victorian harbour town with two grand granite piers made for a bracing seafront stroll and famous ice cream. The James Joyce Tower at nearby Sandycove, where Ulysses opens, is a literary pilgrimage.

A traditional seaside resort at the foot of the Wicklow Mountains, with a long promenade and a cliff walk on to the pretty village of Greystones. The end of the line, and the gateway to the mountains beyond.

A 6th-century monastic city set in a glacial valley of two dark lakes and a near-perfect round tower, an hour's drive south through the Wicklow Mountains National Park. The most beautiful day trip from Dublin, best done privately with a guide and a picnic.

A 5,200-year-old passage tomb older than Stonehenge and the Pyramids, aligned so the rising sun floods its inner chamber at the winter solstice. Access is only by guided tour from the visitor centre, best pre-booked, and easily paired with a private driver from the city.

An 800-year-old castle lived in by one family for nearly all that time, set in parkland with a walled botanic garden and butterfly house. A short trip from the city that suits multi-generational groups, castle for the elders, gardens and playground for the young.

A Palladian mansion above one of the world's great gardens, all Italianate terraces, statuary and a lake framed by the Sugarloaf Mountain. Ireland's highest waterfall sits within the estate. A refined half-day, with lunch in the terrace café.

Ireland's finest medieval city, an easy drive or train south, crowned by a great Norman castle and a walkable 'Medieval Mile' of narrow lanes, craft studios and the black-marble St Canice's Cathedral. A full, rewarding day with genuine character.

A gracious Georgian gallery holding Impressionist masterpieces and, extraordinarily, the entire reconstructed studio of Francis Bacon, moved brick by brick from London. A cultured, uncrowded hour off the tourist trail.

A beautiful museum in a pair of Georgian houses celebrating Ireland's literary giants, holding the first copy of Joyce's Ulysses. Elegant, contemplative, with a lovely garden café, it makes the city's UNESCO literary status tangible.

A single Georgian townhouse that tells the whole social history of Dublin, from grand aristocratic home to overcrowded tenement, through the stories of those who lived in each room. A genuinely moving, small-group experience unlike anything else in the city.

Dublin's 'secret garden', a hidden Victorian pleasure ground of a cascade, fountains, a maze and rose garden, tucked behind the National Concert Hall. Locals treasure it precisely because so few tourists find it.

venues.n: Grafton Street pubs — a curated evening
venues.d: The snug Victorian rooms of Kehoe's, the literary ghosts of Davy Byrnes from Ulysses, and the tiled beauty of The Long Hall. A guided literary-pub crawl, or a discreet advisor-arranged route, gives the atmosphere of Dublin's pub culture without the tourist bustle.

Beneath a 17th-century church lie limestone vaults whose dry air has naturally mummified bodies for centuries, including a figure said to be a Crusader. A macabre, memorable curiosity for the adventurous, by guided tour only.

The 82,000-seat home of Gaelic games, Ireland's fiercely amateur national sports, with a museum and an exhilarating rooftop Skyline walk around the stadium rim. A window into a passion no visitor sees coming, and thrilling for older children.

The first new distillery to open in Dublin in over 125 years, in the historic whiskey district, with hands-on tours and inventive small-batch bottlings. A more intimate, craft-led counterpoint to the big-name distilleries.

A meticulously restored middle-class Georgian home of the 1790s, laid out room by room from cellar to attic exactly as it would have been lived in. The most intimate way to understand the elegance behind those famous Dublin doors.

The largest Anglo-Norman castle in Ireland, a mighty 12th-century keep on the River Boyne where Braveheart was filmed. Often combined with Newgrange on a Boyne Valley day, it rewards those who love history with room to roam.

venues.a: St Stephen's Green — inside The Shelbourne
venues.d: The horseshoe-shaped bar of The Shelbourne — for generations the room where Irish politics, journalism and society have met over a drink.
The glamorous, 1920s-inspired cocktail bar of The Westbury, just off Grafton Street — polished service and beautifully balanced classics.

venues.a: Dublin 1 — Green Street, near the Four Courts
venues.d: A warm, community-minded bar dedicated to reviving poitín — the once-banned Irish spirit — from Dave Mulligan, founder of the Bán poitín brand.
An unmarked, three-storey speakeasy in the heart of Temple Bar — 1920s decor, low light and one of the most acclaimed cocktail lists in the country.

venues.n: The Rooftop Bar at Anantara The Marker
venues.d: The best true rooftop in the city, atop Anantara The Marker — 360° views over the Docklands to the Dublin mountains and the sea.

venues.a: City centre — South Great George's Street
venues.d: One of the most beautiful pub interiors in Dublin — Victorian mirrors, gas-era lamps and a long mahogany bar, largely unchanged for a century and a half.

venues.a: Grafton Street quarter — South Anne Street
venues.d: The pub photographers seek out when they want to show a real Dublin bar — an intact Victorian pub-grocer with original snugs and mahogany drawers.
A Georgian-fronted, Victorian-interior pub that was the mid-century headquarters of Dublin's writers and journalists — and one of the city's great whiskey bars.
A fine example of Victorian pub architecture near the government buildings — its snugs long the unofficial debating chamber of Irish politics and finance.
